sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: Users in a branch office must map a drive letter to an SMB Azure file share hosted at contososa.file.core.windows.net. The branch firewall currently denies all outbound traffic that is not explicitly allowed. Which outbound TCP port must you permit so that the SMB mount succeeds?
spiegazione: SMB access to an Azure file share requires TCP port 445 to the storage account endpoint; this is the single most common cause of mount failures because many organizations and ISPs block outbound 445. TCP 443 is wrong: it is the port used by the FileREST/HTTPS protocol (portal, AzCopy, SDKs) and by the Azure File Sync agent, not by an SMB drive mapping. TCP 2049 is wrong: that is the port used by NFS Azure file shares, and NFS shares cannot be mounted from Windows clients. TCP 3389 is wrong: that is RDP, which has nothing to do with mounting a file share.
tags: azure files, smb, port 445, mount, connectivity

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: A compliance team asks you to configure soft delete for the file shares in storage account sa1 so that an accidentally deleted share stays recoverable for as long as Azure Files allows. What is the maximum retention period you can configure?
spiegazione: Soft delete for Azure file shares supports any retention period between 1 and 365 days, so 365 days is the maximum. 7 days is wrong: that is the default retention period applied to new storage accounts, not the maximum. 30 days is wrong: 30 days is a common default in other Azure services (for example, Recovery Services vault retention) but it is not a limit in Azure Files soft delete. 3,650 days is wrong: 10 years is the maximum period for which you can retain a share snapshot, not a soft delete retention value.
tags: azure files, soft delete, retention, data protection

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: A development team needs an Azure file share that Linux VMs will mount by using the NFS 4.1 protocol. Which storage account configuration supports this requirement?
opzione_a: A StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) account with the Standard_LRS SKU
opzione_b: A FileStorage account with the Premium_LRS SKU
opzione_c: A StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) account with the Standard_GRS SKU
opzione_d: A BlockBlobStorage account with the Premium_ZRS SKU
spiegazione: NFS Azure file shares are available only on the SSD (premium) media tier, which requires the FileStorage storage account kind, and only LRS or ZRS redundancy is supported. A FileStorage account with Premium_LRS therefore meets the requirement. StorageV2 with Standard_LRS is wrong: pay-as-you-go StorageV2 accounts place file shares on the HDD (standard) media tier, which does not support NFS. StorageV2 with Standard_GRS is wrong for the same reason, and geo-redundancy is not even available for NFS shares because NFS requires SSD storage. BlockBlobStorage is wrong: that account kind hosts only blob containers and cannot contain file shares at all.
tags: azure files, nfs, filestorage, premium, ssd, redundancy

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: A scheduled script has been creating share snapshots of the SMB file share 'projects' every hour for several weeks. The script now fails whenever it tries to create a new snapshot, although the share is well below its provisioned size. What should you do to allow new snapshots to be created?
opzione_a: Increase the quota of the 'projects' file share
opzione_b: Delete some of the existing share snapshots
opzione_c: Enable the large file shares feature on the storage account
opzione_d: Move the 'projects' share to the SSD (premium) media tier
spiegazione: Azure Files supports a maximum of 200 share snapshots per file share. After that limit is reached, new snapshot creation fails until older snapshots are deleted, which matches the symptom of an hourly job failing after several weeks. Increasing the share quota is wrong: snapshots do not count toward the maximum size limit of the share, and the stem already states the share is below its provisioned size. Enabling large file shares is wrong: that legacy setting only allowed pay-as-you-go shares to grow beyond 5 TiB; it has no effect on the snapshot count limit. Moving to the SSD (premium) tier is wrong: the 200-snapshot limit applies to every classic file share regardless of media tier, and a share cannot be moved between media tiers in place anyway.
tags: azure files, share snapshots, limits, 200 snapshots

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: On an Azure File Sync server endpoint, cloud tiering is enabled with a volume free space policy of 20 percent and a date policy of 60 days. An administrator observes that files accessed only two days ago are being tiered to the cloud. Which statement explains this behavior?
opzione_a: The volume free space policy takes precedence over the date policy, so files are tiered as needed to reach the free space target regardless of how recently they were accessed
opzione_b: The date policy takes precedence, so the volume free space policy is ignored whenever a date policy is configured
opzione_c: When both policies are configured, Azure File Sync tiers only files that satisfy both policies at the same time
opzione_d: Cloud tiering ignores both policies during the first 60 days after the server endpoint is created
spiegazione: Microsoft documents that the volume free space policy takes precedence over the date policy: Azure File Sync tiers files as needed to reach the configured free space target, even if those files were accessed recently, selecting the coolest files first based on the heatmap. Option b is wrong: the precedence is the opposite, and the volume free space policy is never ignored. Option c is wrong: the policies are not evaluated as an AND condition; either policy on its own can cause a file to be tiered. Option d is wrong: no such grace period exists. Cloud tiering evaluates policy compliance approximately every 60 minutes, and during initial upload the volume free space policy still applies in low disk space mode.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, volume free space policy, date policy

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: FS1 is a Windows Server 2022 file server with an Azure File Sync server endpoint on D:\Data. Cloud tiering is enabled on the server endpoint. The operations team backs up D:\Data by using a third-party file-level backup agent installed on FS1. During a restore test, several recovered files turn out to contain only reparse-point stubs rather than real data. You must give the team a supported way to back up this data set with an on-premises backup product. What should you recommend?
opzione_a: Perform the backups from another server in the same sync group that has cloud tiering disabled
opzione_b: Enable bare-metal restore for FS1 so that tiered files are captured in the system image
opzione_c: Set the volume free space policy on FS1 to 99 percent so that all files are tiered before each backup runs
opzione_d: Configure the backup agent to skip any file that has the offline attribute set
spiegazione: Microsoft states that you should not use solutions that directly back up a server endpoint or a VM containing a server endpoint when cloud tiering is enabled, because tiered files are backed up as stubs. If you prefer an on-premises backup solution, perform the backups on a server in the sync group that has cloud tiering disabled so that the full data set is present locally. Option b is wrong: bare-metal restore, VM restore, and system restore are explicitly not supported when cloud tiering is enabled and can cause unexpected results. Option c is wrong: tiering more files makes the problem worse, since even more files would be backed up as stubs. Option d is wrong: skipping offline files would silently exclude the tiered data from the backup, producing an incomplete backup rather than a usable one.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, backup, tiered files, reparse point

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: Soft delete for file shares is enabled on storage account sa1 with a 90-day retention period. A test file share named 'temp01' was deleted this morning and is now listed in a soft deleted state. Because 'temp01' contained confidential test data, you must remove it permanently today, without waiting for the retention period to expire. Which sequence of actions achieves this?
opzione_a: Undelete 'temp01', disable soft delete on the storage account, and then delete 'temp01' again
opzione_b: Change the soft delete retention period on sa1 to 1 day and wait until the following day
opzione_c: Delete the storage account sa1 and then re-create it with the same name
opzione_d: Apply a CanNotDelete lock to sa1 and then purge the share from the Snapshots blade
spiegazione: Microsoft documents exactly this procedure: to permanently delete a file share that is in a soft deleted state before its expiry time, you must undelete the share, disable soft delete, and then delete the share again (you can re-enable soft delete afterwards to protect the other shares). Option b is wrong: shares deleted before a retention period update expire based on the retention period that was configured when the data was deleted, so lowering the setting to 1 day does not shorten the existing 90-day clock for 'temp01'. Option c is wrong: deleting and re-creating a storage account is destructive to every other share in it and is not the documented method. Option d is wrong: a CanNotDelete lock prevents deletion rather than enabling it, and in fact locks must be removed before snapshots or shares can be deleted; the Snapshots blade has no purge action for soft deleted shares.
tags: azure files, soft delete, undelete, permanent delete, retention

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: SyncGroup1 belongs to Storage Sync Service SSS1 and uses the Azure file share 'projects' as its cloud endpoint. A server endpoint on FS1 already syncs D:\Projects with that cloud endpoint. A second file server, FS2, must now serve exactly the same 'projects' data set to a different office. What should you do?
opzione_a: Add a server endpoint on FS2 to SyncGroup1
opzione_b: Create SyncGroup2 in SSS1, set its cloud endpoint to the 'projects' share, and add a server endpoint on FS2
opzione_c: Add a second cloud endpoint to SyncGroup1 that points to the 'projects' share, and add a server endpoint on FS2
opzione_d: Register FS2 with a second Storage Sync Service and create a sync group there that uses the 'projects' share
spiegazione: A sync group contains exactly one cloud endpoint (the Azure file share) and one or more server endpoints, and all endpoints in the sync group stay in sync with each other. To have FS2 serve the same data, you simply add another server endpoint on FS2 to the existing SyncGroup1. Option b is wrong: a sync group cannot use a cloud endpoint (Azure file share) that is already configured in another sync group. Option c is wrong: a sync group supports only a single cloud endpoint, so you cannot add a second one. Option d is wrong for two reasons: the 'projects' share is already a cloud endpoint in SyncGroup1 and cannot be reused in another sync group, and a server or cluster can be registered with only one Storage Sync Service at a time.
tags: azure file sync, sync group, cloud endpoint, server endpoint, topology

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: Your team is designing a data protection plan that relies on Azure Files share snapshots. Which statements about share snapshots are correct? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Share snapshots are incremental: only the data that changed since the most recent share snapshot is stored
opzione_b: Deleting a file share also deletes all of the share snapshots that were taken of it
opzione_c: You can retain a share snapshot for up to 10 years
opzione_d: You can copy an entire share snapshot to a different storage account in a single operation
opzione_e: The space consumed by share snapshots counts toward the maximum size limit of the file share
spiegazione: Option a is correct: snapshots are incremental, so only content changed since the previous snapshot is saved, which reduces both snapshot creation time and storage cost. Option b is correct: snapshots persist until you explicitly delete them or until the file share is deleted; you cannot delete a share and keep its snapshots, because the delete workflow removes them automatically. Option c is correct: Microsoft documents that you can retain share snapshots for up to 10 years (with a limit of 200 snapshots per share). Option d is incorrect: you cannot copy a whole share snapshot to another storage account; you must copy the data file by file by using AzCopy or a similar mechanism. Option e is incorrect: snapshots do not count toward the maximum share size limit, and there is no limit on the total space that snapshots of a share can consume, although storage account limits still apply.
tags: azure files, share snapshots, incremental, retention, limits

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: You plan to create an Azure File Sync server endpoint with cloud tiering enabled on a new Windows Server 2022 file server. Which requirements must be met for this configuration to be supported? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The path used by the server endpoint must be on a directly attached volume that is formatted with NTFS
opzione_b: The server endpoint path must not be on the Windows system volume
opzione_c: The Azure file share used as the cloud endpoint must use the NFS protocol
opzione_d: The volume must be formatted with ReFS so that the StorageSync.sys filter can create reparse points
opzione_e: The Windows Server instance must be registered with a Storage Sync Service before you can add the server endpoint
spiegazione: Option a is correct: Azure File Sync is supported only on directly attached NTFS volumes. Option b is correct: cloud tiering is explicitly not supported on the Windows system volume. Option e is correct: server endpoints represent paths on registered servers, so you must install the agent and register the server with a Storage Sync Service before you can create a server endpoint in a sync group. Option c is incorrect and is the classic misconception: Azure File Sync supports only SMB Azure file shares. NFS shares (and file shares created with the Microsoft.FileShares resource provider, which are NFS only) are not supported as cloud endpoints. Option d is incorrect: ReFS, FAT, FAT32, and other file systems are not supported; only NTFS is, and it is NTFS that stores the cloud tiering reparse points.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, server endpoint, ntfs, system volume, prerequisites

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: Storage account sa1 hosts several SMB file shares used by different departments. Management asks you to protect the shares against accidental deletion by an administrator, and to keep any deleted share recoverable for the longest period that Azure Files supports. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Level at which soft delete for file shares is configured: [An individual file share | The file service (all file shares in the storage account) | A resource lock on the resource group]
opzione_b: Retention period to configure: [7 days | 90 days | 365 days]
opzione_c: Soft delete can recover an individual file that a user deleted from inside a share: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: Feature to add if individual deleted files must also be recoverable: [Share snapshots | Object replication | Blob versioning]
risposta_corretta: The file service (all file shares in the storage account),365 days,No,Share snapshots
spiegazione: Soft delete for file shares is enabled at the storage account (file service) level, so the setting applies to every file share in the account; it is not a per-share property. The supported retention range is 1 to 365 days, so 365 days is the longest period available (7 days is only the default for new accounts). Soft delete works at the file share level only: undeleting a share restores the share and all of its contents including snapshots, but it cannot recover a single file deleted from within a live share. To recover individual files, Microsoft directs you to share snapshots or Azure file share backup. Object replication and blob versioning are Blob Storage features and do not apply to Azure Files at all. A resource lock is a valid complementary control against deletion but is not where soft delete is configured.
tags: azure files, soft delete, file service, retention, share snapshots

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: A Linux-based analytics workload running on VMs in VNet1 must store data on an Azure file share that is mounted with NFS 4.1. The share must not be reachable from the public internet, and the mount target must keep a static IP address inside VNet1. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Storage account kind and SKU: [StorageV2 with Standard_LRS | FileStorage with Premium_LRS | FileStorage with Premium_GRS]
opzione_b: Protocol to select when you create the file share: [SMB | NFS]
opzione_c: TCP port the Linux clients must be able to reach: [443 | 445 | 2049]
opzione_d: Network configuration to use: [Enable access from all networks on the public endpoint | Create a private endpoint for the storage account in VNet1 | Add an IP address rule for the VM public IPs]
risposta_corretta: FileStorage with Premium_LRS,NFS,2049,Create a private endpoint for the storage account in VNet1
spiegazione: NFS Azure file shares require the SSD (premium) media tier, which means the FileStorage account kind, and only LRS or ZRS redundancy is supported, so FileStorage with Premium_LRS is correct. Premium_GRS is not a valid option because geo-redundancy is not available for NFS shares. StorageV2 with Standard_LRS places shares on the HDD (standard) tier, which does not support NFS. An individual Azure file share supports either SMB or NFS but never both, so NFS must be selected at share creation time. NFS uses TCP 2049 (445 is SMB and 443 is FileREST/HTTPS). NFS shares are never accessible over an unrestricted public endpoint; you must use a private endpoint or a service endpoint. Because the requirement calls for a static IP address, a private endpoint is the correct choice, as service endpoints do not guarantee a stable underlying IP. IP address rules are not supported for NFS Azure file shares.
tags: azure files, nfs, private endpoint, port 2049, filestorage, premium

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: During a hybrid file server rollout, you are adding a server endpoint for E:\Departments on a registered Windows Server 2022 instance. Volume E: is a 500 GiB directly attached NTFS volume formatted with a 4 KiB cluster size. The business requires that at least 20 percent of volume E: always remains free, and that files not accessed for 30 days are moved to the cloud to free local capacity. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Volume free space policy to configure: [10% | 20% | 80%]
opzione_b: Date policy to configure: [7 days | 30 days | 365 days]
opzione_c: Smallest file size that cloud tiering will tier on this volume: [4 KiB | 8 KiB | 64 KiB]
opzione_d: Policy that takes precedence when both are configured: [Date policy | Volume free space policy]
spiegazione: The volume free space policy specifies the percentage of the volume that Azure File Sync keeps free, so requiring at least 20 percent free means setting the policy to 20%. The date policy tiers cool files that have not been accessed (read or written) for the specified number of days, so 30 days matches the requirement. The minimum file size eligible for cloud tiering is calculated as 2x the volume cluster size, with an absolute floor of 8 KiB. On a 4 KiB cluster the calculation gives 8 KiB, so 8 KiB is correct; 4 KiB is below the documented absolute minimum, and 64 KiB would be the threshold for a 32 KiB cluster size. When both policies are configured, the volume free space policy takes precedence: Azure File Sync tiers files as needed to reach the free space target regardless of recent access, so the date policy cannot prevent that tiering.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, volume free space policy, date policy, cluster size, minimum tier size

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda:
Storage account sa1 is a StorageV2 account that contains an SMB file share named 'legal'. Soft delete for file shares is enabled on sa1 with a retention period of 14 days, and the 'legal' share currently has 12 share snapshots. Three days ago, a user permanently deleted an important document from inside the 'legal' share; the share itself was never deleted. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is correct.
1. Soft delete allows you to undelete the individual document that the user removed from the 'legal' share.
2. If an administrator deletes the entire 'legal' share and you undelete it within 14 days, the share is restored together with its 12 share snapshots.
3. If you now change the soft delete retention period on sa1 to 30 days, any share that was already deleted before you made the change will be retained for 30 days from its deletion.
opzione_a: Soft delete allows you to undelete the individual document that the user removed from the 'legal' share.
opzione_b: If an administrator deletes the entire 'legal' share and you undelete it within 14 days, the share is restored together with its 12 share snapshots.
opzione_c: If you now change the soft delete retention period on sa1 to 30 days, any share that was already deleted before you made the change will be retained for 30 days from its deletion.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: soft delete only works at the file share level. It protects against deleting an entire share, not against deletion or modification of individual files inside a live share. To recover a single file, you would use a share snapshot or Azure file share backup. Statement 2 is Yes: Microsoft documents that when you undelete a file share, the file share and all of its contents, including snapshots, are restored to their state prior to deletion. Statement 3 is No: the retention period clock starts when the file share is deleted, and shares deleted before a retention period update expire based on the retention period that was configured at the time that data was deleted. Changing the setting to 30 days affects only shares deleted after the change.
tags: azure files, soft delete, share snapshots, retention, undelete

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda:
Storage Sync Service SSS1 is deployed in the East US region. A Windows Server 2022 file server named FS1 is registered with SSS1. SyncGroup1 in SSS1 has a cloud endpoint that points to the SMB Azure file share 'share1' and a server endpoint for D:\Data on FS1 with cloud tiering enabled. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is correct.
1. You can add a server endpoint for C:\Windows\Shares on FS1 to SyncGroup1 and enable cloud tiering on it.
2. If you upload a file directly into 'share1' by using the Azure portal, Azure File Sync might take up to 24 hours to detect the change and sync it to FS1, because the change detection job for a cloud endpoint runs only once every 24 hours.
3. You can additionally register FS1 with a second Storage Sync Service named SSS2 so that E:\Archive can sync to an Azure file share managed by SSS2.
opzione_a: You can add a server endpoint for C:\Windows\Shares on FS1 to SyncGroup1 and enable cloud tiering on it.
opzione_b: If you upload a file directly into 'share1' by using the Azure portal, Azure File Sync might take up to 24 hours to detect the change and sync it to FS1, because the change detection job for a cloud endpoint runs only once every 24 hours.
opzione_c: You can additionally register FS1 with a second Storage Sync Service named SSS2 so that E:\Archive can sync to an Azure file share managed by SSS2.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: cloud tiering is explicitly not supported on the Windows system volume, and C:\Windows\Shares is on the system volume. Statement 2 is Yes: changes made directly to a cloud endpoint (the Azure file share) must be discovered by an Azure File Sync change detection job, and that job starts only once every 24 hours. Changes made on a server endpoint are detected immediately by the FileSyncSvc.exe service instead. Statement 3 is No: a server or cluster can be registered with only one Storage Sync Service at a time. After registration, FS1 can participate in multiple sync groups, but only within SSS1; to use SSS2 you would first have to unregister FS1 from SSS1.
tags: azure file sync, storage sync service, registered server, cloud tiering, system volume, change detection

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda:
Case study: Fabrikam runs a Windows Server 2019 file server named FS1 in its Boston datacenter. FS1 hosts departmental shares on D:, a directly attached 1.5 TiB NTFS volume that is now 95 percent full. Most of the data has not been opened in over a year, but users must still be able to browse it. Fabrikam wants to centralize the file data in an Azure file share, stop purchasing additional disks for FS1, and keep Boston users accessing their data at LAN speed through the existing UNC paths and NTFS permissions. Fabrikam's ISP blocks outbound TCP port 445 and this cannot be changed. Fabrikam has no ExpressRoute circuit and does not want to deploy a site-to-site VPN.

Which solution meets Fabrikam's requirements?
opzione_a: On FS1, mount the Azure file share with net use, then re-share the mounted drive to Boston users over SMB
opzione_b: Install the Azure File Sync agent on FS1, register FS1 with a Storage Sync Service, create a sync group whose cloud endpoint is the Azure file share and whose server endpoint is D:\, and enable cloud tiering on the server endpoint
opzione_c: Migrate the data to an NFS Azure file share and mount it on FS1, then re-share it to Boston users over SMB
opzione_d: Create a private endpoint for the storage account and have Boston users map a drive directly to the Azure file share
spiegazione: Azure File Sync is the solution Microsoft recommends for exactly this scenario. It turns FS1 into a fast local cache of the Azure file share: the namespace and hot files stay on D: while cloud tiering replaces cool file content with reparse points, freeing local capacity so no new disks are needed. Users keep the existing UNC paths and Windows ACLs, which Azure File Sync preserves. Critically, the agent communicates with the Storage Sync Service and the Azure file share over HTTPS on port 443, so a blocked outbound port 445 is not an obstacle. Option a is wrong: mounting the share with net use is an SMB client operation that requires outbound TCP 445, which the ISP blocks. Option c is wrong: NFS Azure file shares are not supported on Windows clients, and NFS shares are not reachable over an unrestricted public endpoint. Option d is wrong: a private endpoint gives the storage account a private IP inside an Azure virtual network, but Boston clients would still need a VPN or ExpressRoute to reach that address, and they would still need port 445 for SMB, both of which the scenario excludes.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, port 445, sync group, server endpoint, hybrid file server
